overview.title: End of the residual-net summary; introducing batch normalization
overview.main_topic: The tail of the residual model's summary, the wrap-up of residual connections, and the motivation for normalizing intermediate activations
overview.central_idea: Residual connections let you stack arbitrarily deep networks without vanishing gradients. The next pattern, batch normalization, starts from the familiar idea of normalizing input data (subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation) and asks whether the same thing should be done to the activations inside the network.
overview.importance: This page is the hinge between the two most important ConvNet design patterns of the chapter. It also shows, with a concrete parameter table, what a residual model with 1x1 projection shortcuts costs, and it plants the question that the BatchNormalization layer answers on p.301.
learning_objectives: Read the second half of a Keras functional-model summary, including the `Connected to` column of `Add` layers
Recompute the parameter counts of the 3x3 and 1x1 Conv2D layers and the final Dense layer
Recognize which Conv2D layers in the summary are residual projections (1x1 convolutions) rather than main-path convolutions
State the standard data-normalization formula and what assumption it makes about the data
Explain why normalizing only the input data does not guarantee normalized activations deeper in the network
prerequisites: Residual connections and the residual_block function (pp.296-299)
Feature-wise normalization of input data (p.152, p.203-204)
Mean, standard deviation, and the NumPy `axis` argument

summary:
The page opens with the **second half of the `model.summary()` output** started on p.299, for the small residual ConvNet built from three calls to `residual_block` (filters 32, 64, 128). The rows shown here cover the end of the second block and the whole third block:

- `conv2d_11` is a **1x1 convolution** on the residual path (2,112 parameters) that projects the 32-channel output of `add_2` to 64 channels so it can be added to the main path; `add_3` sums it with `max_pooling2d_2`.
- `conv2d_12` and `conv2d_13` are the two 3x3 convolutions of the third block (128 filters), and `conv2d_14` is another 1x1 projection (64 to 128 channels, 8,320 parameters). Because the third block was built with `pooling=False`, the spatial size stays at 8x8 and `add_4` sums `conv2d_13` and `conv2d_14` directly.
- `GlobalAveragePooling2D` collapses the (8, 8, 128) tensor to a 128-vector, and a `Dense(1)` sigmoid classifier adds 129 parameters. The model totals **297,697 parameters (1.14 MB)**, all trainable.

The authors then close section 9.2: with residual connections, depth is no longer limited by **vanishing gradients**.

Section **9.3 Batch normalization** starts by defining *normalization* broadly, as any method that makes the samples a model sees more similar to one another, which helps learning and generalization. The most common form, used repeatedly earlier in the book, centers data on zero and scales it to unit standard deviation:

`normalized_data = (data - np.mean(data, axis=...)) / np.std(data, axis=...)`

The authors note this implicitly assumes a roughly Gaussian distribution that is being centered and scaled to unit variance. Their key point is that until now normalization happened **only before the data entered the model**. Even if the input to a `Dense` or `Conv2D` stack has zero mean and unit variance, nothing guarantees the outputs of those layers do. The page ends on the question that motivates the rest of the section: *could normalizing intermediate activations help?* The answer, the `BatchNormalization` layer, follows on p.301.

paragraphs.excerpt: With residual connections, you can build networks of arbitrary depth, without having
paragraphs.what_it_says: Residual connections allow networks of arbitrary depth without the vanishing-gradient problem; the text now turns to the next essential ConvNet pattern, batch normalization.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is the conclusion of section 9.2. The shortcut path `x + f(x)` gives the gradient an identity route back to earlier layers, so the signal reaching early layers is not just a long product of small Jacobians. That is why depth stops being the bottleneck. The phrase "arbitrary depth" is the authors' rhetorical summary; in practice very deep nets also need good initialization and, as the next section explains, normalization.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It frames batch normalization as the second of a pair of tools that make deep ConvNets trainable. The book later (p.627) pairs them explicitly: residual connections and batch normalization both help gradient information flow through a deep network.
paragraphs.technical_idea: For y = x + f(x), dy/dx = I + df/dx, so the backpropagated gradient always contains an identity term that does not shrink with depth.

terminology.meaning: The tendency of gradients to shrink toward zero as they are propagated back through many layers, so early layers barely learn.
A reusable structural recipe (residual connection, batch normalization, separable convolution) rather than a specific model.

connections: p.296: residual connections were introduced as the fix for vanishing gradients in deep stacks
p.627: the conclusion chapter groups batch normalization and residual connections as the two patterns for very deep ConvNets

paragraphs.excerpt: Normalization in machine learning is a broad category of methods that seek
paragraphs.what_it_says: Normalization is a family of methods that make samples more similar to one another, aiding learning and generalization. The most common one, seen several times already, subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation, which assumes the data is roughly normal (Gaussian) and centers and scales it to unit variance.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The definition is deliberately broad: normalization is about removing irrelevant variation in scale and offset so that the model's weights can focus on the structure that matters. Standardization (z-scoring) is the special case: each value becomes "how many standard deviations from the mean". The Gaussian remark is a gentle caveat: mean and standard deviation fully describe a Gaussian, so standardizing a Gaussian gives exactly N(0, 1); for skewed or heavy-tailed data, standardization still centers and scales it but does not make it Gaussian.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Batch normalization is exactly this formula, applied inside the network to activations instead of to raw inputs, with the statistics computed per batch. Understanding the input-side version makes the layer straightforward.
paragraphs.technical_idea: z = (x - mu) / sigma, with mu and sigma computed along an axis chosen so that each feature is normalized independently.

terminology.meaning: Any transformation that makes samples more comparable to one another, typically by fixing their location and scale.
The square root of the variance; the typical distance of values from their mean.
Variance (and thus standard deviation) equal to 1 after scaling.

connections: p.152: feature-wise normalization of the Boston housing data, the first time this formula appeared
p.203: the universal workflow recommends small, homogeneous values and optionally per-feature mean 0 / std 1

paragraphs.excerpt: Previous examples you saw in this book normalized data before feeding it
paragraphs.what_it_says: Earlier examples normalized data only before feeding it to the model. But normalization may matter after every transformation: zero-mean, unit-variance inputs to a Dense or Conv2D network do not imply that its outputs have those properties. Could normalizing intermediate activations help?
paragraphs.what_it_means: A layer computes something like relu(W x + b). Even with standardized x, the output's mean is shifted by b and by the ReLU (which outputs only non-negative values, so the mean is positive), and its variance depends on the scale of W. As W changes during training, these statistics drift, so every downstream layer is learning against a moving input distribution. The question at the end proposes treating every layer's input the way we treat the model's input.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the motivation for the `BatchNormalization` layer described on p.301. Note that the authors pose it as a question: they will shortly say that the mechanism by which batch normalization helps is not well understood.
paragraphs.technical_idea: If x has mean 0 and covariance I, then Wx + b has mean b and covariance W W^T; a ReLU then makes the mean strictly positive. Nothing in training keeps these near 0 and I.

terminology.meaning: The outputs of hidden layers, which are the inputs of the following layers.
Before looking at the data or training, from first principles.

connections: p.301: BatchNormalization is introduced as the answer, using batch statistics in training and moving averages at inference
p.469: LayerNormalization, a variant that normalizes each sequence independently, is used in the Transformer

concepts.name: Residual connection
concepts.definition: A shortcut that adds a block's input to its output, y = x + f(x), with a 1x1 convolution on the shortcut when the shapes differ.
concepts.intuition: The block only needs to learn a correction to its input; the unchanged input and its gradient always have a direct path.
concepts.technical: In this summary, conv2d_11 and conv2d_14 are the 1x1 projections on the shortcut (the residual path) because filter counts change from 32 to 64 and from 64 to 128. The Add layers list two inputs in the `Connected to` column.
concepts.significance: Lets the authors claim networks of 'arbitrary depth' without vanishing gradients.
concepts.example: add_4 = conv2d_13 output + conv2d_14(add_3), both of shape (None, 8, 8, 128).
concepts.misconception: A residual connection always costs zero parameters. Only the identity shortcut is free; a projection shortcut has kernel and bias weights (8,320 for conv2d_14).

concepts.name: Data normalization (standardization)
concepts.definition: Subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation so data is centered at 0 with unit variance.
concepts.intuition: Express every value as 'how many standard deviations away from typical' so all features live on the same scale.
concepts.technical: z = (x - mean(x, axis)) / std(x, axis). The axis argument determines which values share statistics, e.g. axis=0 for per-feature normalization of a (samples, features) matrix.
concepts.significance: It is the operation batch normalization performs inside the network.
concepts.example: Values [2, 4, 6]: mean 4, std about 1.633, normalized about [-1.22, 0, 1.22].
concepts.misconception: Standardizing data makes it Gaussian. It only shifts and scales; the shape of the distribution is unchanged.

concepts.name: Batch normalization
concepts.definition: A layer that normalizes intermediate activations using batch statistics during training and moving averages at inference (detailed on p.301).
concepts.intuition: Give every layer the same tidy, centered, unit-scale input that we already give the model's first layer.
concepts.technical: On this page only the motivation appears: inputs normalized at the start do not stay normalized after Dense/Conv2D transformations.
concepts.significance: One of the essential ConvNet patterns of chapter 9; it helps gradient propagation and enables deeper networks (p.301).
concepts.example: See p.301-302 for its use after Conv2D layers.
concepts.misconception: That normalizing inputs once is enough for the whole network. The page argues exactly the opposite.

concepts.name: Global average pooling
concepts.definition: Averaging each channel over all spatial positions, turning (H, W, C) into (C).
concepts.intuition: Summarize 'how much of each feature is present anywhere in the image'.
concepts.technical: Here (None, 8, 8, 128) becomes (None, 128) with zero parameters, so the final Dense layer needs only 128 weights + 1 bias.
concepts.significance: Keeps the classifier head tiny compared with Flatten + Dense (which would need 8*8*128 = 8,192 weights).
concepts.misconception: Pooling layers have trainable weights. They have none.

math.title: Standard data normalization

variables.meaning: Mean of the data along the chosen axis (`np.mean(data, axis=...)`)
Standard deviation along the same axis (`np.std`, which by default divides by N, not N-1)
Number of values the statistics are computed over

math.operations: Subtract the mean (centering), then divide by the standard deviation (scaling). NumPy broadcasting applies the per-axis statistics to every element.
math.purpose: Make the data zero-mean and unit-variance so that features are on comparable scales.
math.interpretation: Each normalized value is a z-score: its signed distance from the mean in units of standard deviation.
math.intuition: Shift the cloud of points to the origin, then shrink or stretch it until its typical spread is 1.
math.numerical_example: For `data = [2, 4, 6]`: $\mu = 4$, $\sigma = \sqrt{(4+0+4)/3} \approx 1.633$, so the output is $\approx [-1.225, 0, 1.225]$, which has mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

math.title: Conv2D parameter counts in the summary

variables.meaning: Kernel height and width (3 for main-path convolutions, 1 for residual projections)
Number of filters (output channels); one bias each

math.operations: Multiply kernel area by input and output channels, add one bias per output channel.
math.purpose: Verify the numbers printed in the summary and see where the parameters live.
math.interpretation: The two 3x3 convolutions of the 128-filter block hold about 74% of all parameters; the 1x1 shortcuts are comparatively cheap.
math.intuition: Parameters grow with the product of input and output channels, so the last, widest block dominates.
math.numerical_example: conv2d_11: $1\cdot1\cdot32\cdot64+64 = 2112$; conv2d_12: $3\cdot3\cdot64\cdot128+128 = 73856$; conv2d_13: $3\cdot3\cdot128\cdot128+128 = 147584$; conv2d_14: $1\cdot1\cdot64\cdot128+128 = 8320$; dense: $128+1 = 129$. With float32 weights, $297697 \times 4$ bytes $\approx 1.19\times10^6$ bytes $\approx 1.14$ MiB, matching the printed size.

code.title: model.summary() output for the residual ConvNet (second part)
code.what_it_does: Shows the remaining rows of the summary started on p.299 (the `>>> model.summary()` call, the header and the rows for the input, rescaling, first block and the main path of the second block are on p.299). These rows cover the second block's residual projection and Add, the full third block, the global pooling and the classifier, followed by the parameter totals.

line_explanations.explanation: conv2d_11: the 1x1 projection of the second block's residual. It reads from add_2 (the first block's output, 16x16x32) and outputs 8x8x64, so it must use strides=2 to match the max-pooled main path (as residual_block does when pooling=True, p.298-299). 1*1*32*64 + 64 = 2,112 parameters.
add_3 sums the main path (max_pooling2d_2) and the projected residual (conv2d_11). Add layers have no parameters; the `Connected to` column lists both inputs.
conv2d_12 and conv2d_13: the two 3x3 convolutions with 128 filters of the third block (residual_block(x, filters=128, pooling=False)). Padding 'same' keeps 8x8.
conv2d_14: a 1x1 projection of add_3 from 64 to 128 channels. No stride is needed because the third block has no pooling; this is the `elif filters != residual.shape[-1]` branch from p.299.
add_4 merges conv2d_13 and conv2d_14, both (8, 8, 128).
GlobalAveragePooling2D reduces each of the 128 channels to its spatial mean: (None, 128), no parameters.
Dense(1, activation='sigmoid'): 128 weights + 1 bias = 129 parameters, a binary classifier.
Totals: 297,697 parameters, all trainable (no BatchNormalization layers yet, which would add non-trainable moving statistics). 1.14 MB is the float32 storage size.

code.inputs_outputs: Input to the model: (None, 32, 32, 3) images (see p.299); output: (None, 1) probability.
code.algorithm: Stack of residual blocks with increasing filter counts (32, 64, 128), downsampling in the first two, followed by global average pooling and a sigmoid Dense head.
code.theory_link: Every block output is an Add of a main path and a (possibly projected) shortcut, which is what keeps gradients flowing in deep stacks.

parameters.name: Param #
parameters.role: Number of weights in the layer (kernel + bias)

parameters.name: Connected to
parameters.role: Which layer outputs feed this layer; two entries for Add layers reveal the residual merges

parameters.name: Non-trainable params
parameters.role: Weights not updated by gradient descent; 0 here, but BatchNormalization layers would contribute their moving mean/variance

pitfalls: Truncated names (`max_pooling2d_2[0]…`, `global_average_poo…`) are just column-width truncation in the printout.
Layer index numbers (conv2d_11 etc.) depend on how many layers were created earlier in the session; they will differ if you rerun in a fresh session.
Do not confuse the 1x1 projection convolutions with main-path convolutions when counting the depth of the network.
code.illustrative_code:
# Beyond the book: recompute the printed parameter counts
def conv_params(k, c_in, c_out):
    return k * k * c_in * c_out + c_out

print(conv_params(1, 32, 64))    # 2112   conv2d_11
print(conv_params(3, 64, 128))   # 73856  conv2d_12
print(conv_params(3, 128, 128))  # 147584 conv2d_13
print(conv_params(1, 64, 128))   # 8320   conv2d_14
print(128 + 1)                   # 129    dense

code.title: The normalization one-liner
code.what_it_does: Centers data on zero and scales it to unit standard deviation along a chosen axis; the `...` is a placeholder for whichever axis holds the samples.

line_explanations.explanation: np.mean and np.std compute statistics along `axis`; broadcasting subtracts and divides them elementwise. With a (samples, features) array and axis=0, each feature column is normalized independently.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: an array `data`; output: an array of the same shape with zero mean and unit std along the chosen axis.
code.theory_link: BatchNormalization performs the same computation on activations, with the batch axis (and, for images, the spatial axes) as the reduction axes.

parameters.name: axis
parameters.role: The axis over which statistics are computed (left as `...` in the book)

pitfalls: Statistics should be computed on the training data only and reused for validation/test data.
A constant feature has std 0 and causes division by zero; real implementations add a small epsilon.
Use keepdims=True or pick the axis carefully so broadcasting lines up.
code.illustrative_code:
# Beyond the book: per-feature normalization of a (samples, features) array
import numpy as np
data = np.array([[2., 100.], [4., 200.], [6., 300.]])
mean = data.mean(axis=0)            # [4., 200.]
std = data.std(axis=0)              # [1.633, 81.65]
print((data - mean) / std)          # each column: [-1.22, 0., 1.22]

deeper.title: Why activations drift even with normalized inputs
deeper.body:
Beyond the book, a quick derivation of the authors' claim:

1. Let $x$ have mean $0$ and covariance $I$.
2. A Dense layer computes $z = Wx + b$. Then $\mathbb{E}[z] = b$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(z) = WW^\top$. Unless $b = 0$ and $W$ is orthogonal, the output is neither zero-mean nor unit-variance.
3. A ReLU then sets negatives to zero, so $\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{relu}(z)] > 0$ and the variance is roughly halved for a symmetric $z$.
4. Each training step changes $W$ and $b$, so these statistics change over time, and the next layer sees a moving target.

This drift is what the original batch-norm paper called *internal covariate shift*. The book (p.301) notes that this explanation is a hypothesis, not established fact.

deeper.title: Thermostat analogy
deeper.body: Normalizing only the input is like setting a building's thermostat only at the front door: by the time air has passed through several rooms with open windows and heaters, each room is at a different temperature. Putting a thermostat in each room (a normalization layer after each transformation) keeps every room in a comfortable range regardless of what happened upstream.

deeper.title: Where the 297,697 parameters live
deeper.body: Adding the rows from pp.299-300: block 1 has 896 + 9,248 + 128 (projection) = 10,272; block 2 has 18,496 + 36,928 + 2,112 = 57,536; block 3 has 73,856 + 147,584 + 8,320 = 229,760; head has 129. Sum: 297,697. Block 3 holds about 77% of the model because its 3x3 convolutions connect 64 or 128 input channels to 128 outputs. This is typical: parameter cost concentrates in the widest, deepest blocks, which is one motivation for the cheaper separable convolutions of section 9.4 (p.302).

misconceptions.claim: If the input data is normalized, the whole network sees normalized data.
misconceptions.correction: The page states the opposite: there is no reason to expect a priori that the outputs of a Dense or Conv2D layer keep zero mean and unit variance.

misconceptions.claim: Mean/std normalization turns any data into a Gaussian.
misconceptions.correction: It only shifts and rescales. The authors say it assumes the data is (roughly) Gaussian; it does not make it so.

misconceptions.claim: Every Conv2D in the summary is a layer of depth.
misconceptions.correction: conv2d_11 and conv2d_14 are 1x1 projections on the residual shortcuts, used only to match channel counts before the Add.

takeaways: The residual model totals 297,697 parameters; most sit in the 128-filter block's two 3x3 convolutions.
Rows with a 1x1 Conv2D reading from an Add layer are residual projections that match channel counts.
Residual connections remove depth as a practical limit imposed by vanishing gradients.
Normalization = making samples more similar; the standard form subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation.
Normalizing inputs does not keep activations normalized after Dense or Conv2D transformations, which motivates normalizing intermediate activations.

questions.question: Verify the parameter count of conv2d_13 (Conv2D, 128 filters, 3x3 kernel, input from conv2d_12 with 128 channels).
questions.explanation: A Conv2D has k_h*k_w*C_in*C_out kernel weights plus one bias per filter. This matches the printed 147,584.

questions.question: Why does conv2d_14 have only 8,320 parameters while conv2d_12, which also maps 64 to 128 channels, has 73,856?
options: conv2d_14 is a 1x1 convolution on the residual path, conv2d_12 a 3x3 main-path convolution
conv2d_14 shares its weights with conv2d_12
questions.answer: conv2d_14 is a 1x1 convolution on the residual path, conv2d_12 a 3x3 main-path convolution
questions.explanation: 1*1*64*128+128 = 8,320 vs 3*3*64*128+128 = 73,856: the factor of 9 comes from kernel area. Bias is present in both, stride does not change parameter count, and Keras layers do not share weights here.

questions.question: In the book's words, what is normalization in machine learning?
questions.answer: A broad category of methods that seek to make different samples seen by a model more similar to each other, helping it learn and generalize to new data.
questions.explanation: This is the definition at the start of section 9.3; mean/std standardization is the most common instance.

questions.question: The input to a Dense layer has zero mean and unit variance. Give two reasons its output after a ReLU will generally not.
questions.answer: The bias b and the weights W shift and rescale the data (mean b, covariance WW^T), and ReLU discards negative values so the mean becomes positive. Both also change as weights are updated during training.
questions.explanation: This expands the authors' statement that there is no a priori reason for outputs to stay normalized, which motivates normalizing intermediate activations.

questions.question: What assumption do the authors say mean/std normalization makes about the data?
options: That it follows a normal (Gaussian) distribution
That it lies in the 0-1 range
questions.answer: That it follows a normal (Gaussian) distribution
questions.explanation: The page says it 'makes the assumption that the data follows a normal (or Gaussian) distribution' and centers and scales it to unit variance. The 0-1 range belongs to rescaling (p.203); uniformity and independence are not mentioned.

questions.question: Normalize the values [1, 3, 5, 7] with the page's formula (np.std divides by N).
questions.explanation: Deviations are -3, -1, 1, 3; squared mean (9+1+1+9)/4 = 5; dividing each deviation by sqrt(5) gives the z-scores.

questions.question: Can you point to every residual merge in the model summary on pp.299-300 and say which layer is the main path and which is the shortcut?
questions.answer: add_2: max_pooling2d_1 (main) + conv2d_8 (shortcut); add_3: max_pooling2d_2 (main) + conv2d_11 (shortcut); add_4: conv2d_13 (main) + conv2d_14 (shortcut).
questions.explanation: Shortcut layers are the 1x1 Conv2D layers whose input is the previous block's output (rescaling, add_2, add_3).
